title: The Qiskit Primitives
summary: Sampler returns counts from shots, Estimator returns expectation values of observables, and the statistical error falls as 1/√shots.
objectives: Get the same expectation value in two ways: directly, and from counts
Measure an X-type observable using only computational-basis measurements
Say how many shots a given precision costs
mission: Counts are only useful once they become a number. For the Bell state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 in qc, store in zz_est and xx_est the values of ⟨Z⊗Z⟩ and ⟨X⊗X⟩ from the Estimator. Then compute the same two values from Sampler counts, in zz_samp and xx_samp, and ⟨Z⟩ of qubit 0 from counts in z0_samp. Store in sigma the statistical error 1/√shots of a Z expectation value.

prediction.question: With 4096 shots the statistical error of ⟨Z⟩ for a qubit in |+⟩ is about 0.016. Roughly how many shots do you need to bring it down to 0.004?
prediction.explanation: The error is 1/√N. Going from 0.016 to 0.004 divides it by 4, so N must be multiplied by 4² = 16, which is 65536 shots. Four times the shots would only halve the error; the idea that the error falls in proportion to the shots is what makes the cost of precision easy to underestimate.

hints: The Sampler only measures in the computational basis. What do you have to add to a copy of qc before you can read counts from it, and what does each outcome contribute to ⟨Z⊗Z⟩?

Each outcome counts +1 if the two bits are equal and −1 if they differ. For ⟨X⊗X⟩ the counts of qc itself are no use: put a Hadamard gate on both qubits of a copy first, because H X H = Z, then use the same rule. The Estimator takes the observable in the PUB, SparsePauliOp('XX'), and needs no rotation.

For ⟨Z⟩ of qubit 0 only the bit of qubit 0 counts, and in a key such as '10' that is the rightmost character. For sigma, an average of ±1 results with mean 0 has error 1/√shots. Keep qc itself without measurements: the measured copies are separate circuits.

messages.ok: All values agree. With this many shots the statistical error is {sigma}, and your ⟨Z⟩ of qubit 0 from counts is {z0}, a fluctuation of about that size around 0.
messages.no_circuit: There is no circuit in qc yet. Build the Bell state with a Hadamard gate on qubit 0 and a CNOT.
messages.wrong_state: qc does not prepare the Bell state: the fidelity with (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 is {fidelity}. Check the gates, and leave the measurements for copies of qc.
messages.missing: {name} is not defined yet. Store the result in the variable {name}.
messages.wrong_est: The Estimator gives {actual} for {name}, but the Bell state has exactly 1. Check the observable you passed: its string should have one letter per qubit.
messages.bad_shots: shots is {shots}. Use between 1000 and 100000, so that the error is small enough to see and the run stays fast.
messages.wrong_sigma: sigma is {actual}, but 1/√shots is {want}. Remember the square root, and use the same shots as the Sampler.
messages.wrong_samp: {name} from counts is {actual}, farther from 1 than shot noise allows. If it is ⟨X⊗X⟩ and you read the Z-basis counts, that is the probable slip: apply a Hadamard gate to both qubits before measuring. Otherwise check the sign rule (equal bits give +1).
messages.wrong_z0: z0_samp is {actual}, but the exact value is 0 and shot noise should keep it within {limit}. You probably used both bits, which gives ⟨Z⊗Z⟩. Use only the bit of qubit 0, the rightmost character of each outcome.

challenge.mission: The mission read ⟨X⊗X⟩ by putting a Hadamard gate on both qubits before measuring. Y needs a different change, and a function that does it for any label saves rewriting the circuit each time. Write pauli_from_counts(qc, pauli, sampler): qc is a two-qubit circuit without measurements, pauli is a label of two letters from I, X, Y and Z, and sampler is a Sampler that runs your circuit with its own shots. Return the estimate of the expectation value of that Pauli operator in the state qc prepares, computed from counts. The label follows Qiskit's convention for SparsePauliOp: the rightmost letter acts on qubit 0 and the leftmost on qubit 1, and an I leaves that qubit out of the parity. The validator calls your function on three states and nine labels of its own, with a seeded sampler of 20000 shots, and accepts each estimate within 0.032 of the exact value (4.5 standard errors). It also checks that your function leaves the circuit it was given unchanged. The Bell state qc of the mission is a case to test on.
hints: Which single-qubit gate sends the eigenstates of X to those of Z? For Y the same gate is not enough: the eigenstates of Y are (|0⟩ ± i|1⟩)/√2, and the phase i has to be removed first.
Apply S† and then H to read Y, H alone to read X, nothing for Z. Loop over the letters of the label: the letter at position p of a string of length n acts on qubit n − 1 − p.

Collect the qubits whose letter is not I. For each outcome in the counts, the sign is (−1) to the number of 1s among the bits of those qubits, and bits[-1 - q] is the bit of qubit q. Work on qc.copy() and measure that copy.

messages.ok: pauli_from_counts reproduced all nine expectation values; the largest deviation from the exact value was {worst}, inside the limit of {limit}.
messages.ch_no_function: There is no function pauli_from_counts(qc, pauli, sampler) yet.
messages.ch_error: pauli_from_counts raised an exception for the label {label}: {error}. A common cause is measuring a circuit that already has measurements, or indexing a letter of the label with the wrong qubit.
messages.ch_bad_return: For the label {label} the function did not return a finite number. It should return the average of the ±1 values.
messages.ch_modified: After the call with the label {label} the circuit you were given has more instructions than before. Add the basis changes and the measurements to a copy of it.
messages.ch_sign: For {label} you returned {actual} and the exact value is {exact}: same size, opposite sign. This is what happens when Y is read with a Hadamard gate alone, or with S where S† is needed. S† and then H takes the +1 eigenstate of Y to |0⟩.
messages.ch_identity: For {label} you returned {actual} and the exact value is {exact}. A letter I means that qubit carries no sign, so only the bits of the other qubit enter the parity. Check which bits you count, and which qubit each letter belongs to.
messages.ch_wrong: For {label} you returned {actual} and the exact value is {exact}, farther apart than shot noise allows (about {limit}). Check the basis change on each qubit and that the leftmost letter of the label belongs to qubit 1.
